en.title: Biochemistry: the whole course
en.short: What biochemistry covers, how biochemistry degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What biochemistry is
sections.text: Biochemistry is the study of the molecules and chemical reactions of living organisms. It asks how proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids are built, how they behave, and how cells obtain and use energy. It also asks how information stored in DNA becomes working molecules, and how those processes are controlled. Biochemistry sits between chemistry and biology. It uses chemical ideas such as bonding, equilibrium, redox and thermodynamics to explain biological events, and it uses laboratory methods to test those explanations. The subject supports medicine, agriculture, pharmacy, food science and biotechnology. These notes teach principles and standard laboratory reasoning. They do not replace your department’s handbook, safety rules or a qualified supervisor.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text: Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, biochemistry is commonly studied as a four-year BSc, and many programmes include a period of industrial training under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Some polytechnics offer related ND and HND courses in science laboratory technology rather than a degree named biochemistry. In the United Kingdom a BSc usually takes three years, with an integrated master’s often taking four; in Scotland each usually takes a year longer. Ghana and Kenya have their own patterns. A master’s degree usually adds advanced taught modules and a research dissertation, and a PhD is based on original research. Always confirm the current duration, entry requirements and award title with your institution.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
The early topics build the language: general chemistry for bonding, equilibrium and redox; organic chemistry of biomolecules; analytical chemistry and the laboratory; mathematics and statistics; cell biology and compartmentation; amino acids and peptides; protein structure and function; the structure and properties of carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids. These topics explain what the molecules are and how their shapes matter.

The core topics follow the logic of metabolism and information flow. Enzymes, including kinetics, inhibition and regulation, and bioenergetics come first, then glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, photosynthesis and carbon fixation. Next are glycogen metabolism and the pentose phosphate pathway, lipid metabolism, and nitrogen metabolism for amino acids and nucleotides. Molecular biology follows: DNA replication and repair, transcription and RNA processing, translation, gene regulation and epigenetics. Membrane transport and signal transduction connect the cell to its environment. Biochemical and molecular biology techniques, metabolic integration and clinical biochemistry, and research ethics and biosafety complete the core.

At master’s level, students study advanced enzymology and protein dynamics, genomics, proteomics and bioinformatics, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text: Learn structures by drawing them from memory, then check against a correct diagram. Do the same for pathways: write the name, substrate, product, enzyme, cofactor and one control point. Understanding the purpose of a pathway makes the details easier to hold. Use short, spaced revision rather than one long reading. Work numerical problems in enzyme kinetics, pH and buffers, thermodynamics and statistics, and write units on every line. In the laboratory, read the protocol before the class, record raw data at the time, and calculate results soon afterwards. Link each pathway to a clinical or real example, such as why an enzyme defect causes a particular sign. Use your lecture notes, a standard textbook and past questions together. Ask your lecturer which textbook and which edition the course follows.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Memorising names without understanding the chemistry is the main error. Students also confuse similar molecules and pathways, such as glycolysis with gluconeogenesis, or replication with transcription. They skip the chemistry of pH, redox and bonding, then struggle with enzyme and energy topics. Many neglect units and significant figures in calculations. In the laboratory, common faults are not reading the protocol, not labelling samples, and leaving calculations until the report is due. Some students study pathways in isolation and miss how they are controlled and integrated. Finally, do not rely on summaries alone. Use them to organise your learning, then go back to your handbook, lectures and textbook for the detail your course requires.

keyPoints: Biochemistry explains the molecules and chemical reactions of living organisms using chemistry and laboratory evidence.
Degree length and award titles vary by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
The course moves from molecular building blocks to enzymes, metabolism, molecular biology and integrated clinical biochemistry.
Draw structures and pathways from memory, and understand the purpose of each step.
Write units on every line and check that numerical answers are reasonable.
Laboratory safety, accurate records and research ethics are part of the subject, not extras.

en.title: General chemistry for biochemistry: bonding, equilibrium and redox
en.short: Atomic structure, periodic trends, bonding, intermolecular forces, acids, equilibrium and redox in biochemistry.

sections.heading: Atomic structure and trends
sections.text:
Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in orbitals. Atomic number Z is the proton count; mass number A is protons plus neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A.

Across a period, effective nuclear charge rises, so atomic radius falls while electronegativity and ionisation energy rise. Down a group, extra shells increase radius and lower electronegativity. These trends explain ion formation and bond polarity.

sections.heading: Bonding and forces
sections.text:
Ionic bonding transfers electrons and holds ions together by electrostatic attraction, as in Na+ Cl−. Covalent bonding shares an electron pair. Unequal sharing gives a polar covalent bond with partial charges.

Intermolecular forces are weaker attractions between molecules: London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonds. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules, and between polar groups in biomolecules, affect solubility and shape.

sections.heading: Acids, bases and equilibrium
sections.text:
A Brønsted acid donates a proton and a base accepts one. pH = −log[H+]. For a weak acid HA, Ka = [H+][A−] ÷ [HA]. At equilibrium, the reaction quotient Q compared with K shows the direction; K changes with temperature. A buffer follows pH = pKa + log([A−] ÷ [HA]).

Example: 0.10 M HA with Ka = 1.8 × 10^-5. [H+] ≈ √(Ka × C) = √(1.8 × 10^-6) = 1.34 × 10^-3 M, so pH = −log(1.34 × 10^-3) = 2.87.

sections.heading: Redox reactions
sections.text:
Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain. A redox reaction transfers electrons from a reducing agent to an oxidising agent. Biological examples include NAD+ being reduced to NADH, and two cysteine thiol groups being oxidised to a disulfide bond.

Redox potentials compare electron affinity: a positive cell potential means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.

keyPoints: Atomic number is the proton count; isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass number.
Across a period atomic radius falls and electronegativity rises; down a group radius rises and electronegativity falls.
Ionic bonds transfer electrons; covalent bonds share them, and unequal sharing gives polar bonds.
Weak acid: Ka = [H+][A−] ÷ [HA], and pH = −log[H+].
Buffer: pH = pKa + log([A−] ÷ [HA]).
Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain; NAD+ is reduced to NADH in many biological reactions.

en.title: Organic chemistry of biomolecules
en.short: Carbon bonding, functional groups, isomerism, stereochemistry and the main reaction types.

sections.heading: Carbon bonding
sections.text:
Carbon has four valence electrons, so it forms four covalent bonds. It bonds to itself in chains and rings, and to hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus. Single bonds give tetrahedral sp3 carbon, double bonds trigonal planar sp2 carbon, and triple bonds linear sp carbon. This lets biomolecules form stable, varied skeletons.

A functional group is an atom or group of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic reactions. Common groups include hydroxyl (−OH), carbonyl (C=O), carboxyl (−COOH), amino (−NH₂), phosphate, sulfhydryl (−SH), ester and amide. The skeleton affects size and shape, but functional groups often decide solubility, acidity and reactivity.

sections.heading: Isomerism and stereochemistry
sections.text:
Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity. For example, lactic acid and glyceraldehyde both have the formula C₃H₆O₃, but their atoms are joined differently. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement. Enantiomers are mirror images; diastereomers are not mirror images; cis-trans isomers differ around a double bond or ring.

A chiral carbon is attached to four different groups. Lactic acid has one chiral carbon, so it exists as two enantiomers. Enantiomers often behave differently in living systems because enzymes are themselves chiral.

sections.heading: Reaction types
sections.text:
Substitution replaces one atom or group by another. In nucleophilic substitution, a nucleophile donates electrons to an electron-poor carbon while a leaving group departs with the bonding electrons. SN2 is one step; SN1 goes through a carbocation, a carbon with a positive charge. Elimination removes two groups and forms a double bond, often by dehydration. Addition adds groups across a double or triple bond, as in hydrogenation of an alkene.

Carbonyl reactions are central. The C=O bond is polar, with a partial positive carbon, so nucleophiles add there. Alcohols add to aldehydes and ketones to form hemiacetals, a carbon bonded to OH and OR. A second alcohol gives an acetal. Amines can form imines (C=N compounds). These reactions help explain sugar ring formation and many enzyme mechanisms.

keyPoints: Carbon is tetravalent and forms stable chains and rings with single, double or triple bonds.
Functional groups such as hydroxyl, carbonyl, carboxyl, amino and phosphate determine a molecule’s reactions.
Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity or spatial arrangement.
A chiral carbon has four different groups and gives enantiomers, which can behave differently in biology.
Substitution replaces a group, elimination forms a double bond, and addition adds groups across a multiple bond.
The polar C=O bond attracts nucleophiles, explaining hemiacetal, acetal and imine formation.

en.title: Analytical chemistry and the biochemistry laboratory
en.short: Units, significant figures, concentration, titration, pH, spectroscopy, chromatography, safety and error.

sections.heading: Measurement and units
sections.text: Science uses SI units: metre, kilogram, second, mole, kelvin. A quantity is a number with a unit; write both. Significant figures are the digits that carry meaning. In multiplication and division, keep the least number of significant figures in the inputs. In addition and subtraction, keep the least number of decimal places. Example: 12.34 g + 0.567 g = 12.907 g, rounded to 12.91 g because 12.34 has two decimal places. Do not report more digits than the instrument supports.

sections.heading: Solutions and titration
sections.text: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution: c = n ÷ V, with V in litres. A 0.100 M solution contains 0.100 mol in 1.000 L. In acid-base titration, a standard solution of known concentration neutralises an unknown. At the equivalence point, moles react in the ratio of the balanced equation. Example: 25.0 cm³ HCl needs 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 M NaOH. n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol. The equation HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O is 1:1, so n(HCl) = 0.00200 mol. c(HCl) = 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 M.

sections.heading: pH and spectroscopy
sections.text: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is in mol/L. A pH meter must be calibrated with fresh buffer solutions. Spectroscopy measures absorption of light. The Beer-Lambert law is A = εcl, where A is absorbance, ε the molar absorptivity, c concentration and l path length. Absorbance is linear in concentration only over a calibrated range.

sections.heading: Chromatography, safety and error
sections.text: Chromatography separates substances between a mobile phase and a stationary phase. In thin-layer chromatography, Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent front. Laboratory safety needs a risk assessment, personal protective equipment, a fume hood for volatile solvents, labelled waste and knowledge of local rules. Experimental error is random (scatter) or systematic (bias). Calibration reduces systematic error; repeat measurements reduce random error. Report mean and standard deviation, and state units.

keyPoints: Write every measurement with its SI unit, and in calculations keep the least number of significant figures or decimal places.
Molarity is c = n ÷ V, with V in litres.
In titration, moles react in the ratio of the balanced equation.
pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], with [H⁺] in mol/L.
The Beer-Lambert law is A = εcl.
Random error scatters results, systematic error shifts them, and calibration and repeats help.

en.title: Mathematics and statistics for biochemistry
en.short: Logs, exponentials, rates, graphs, units, descriptive statistics, uncertainty and basic hypothesis testing.

sections.heading: Logs and exponentials
sections.text: A logarithm answers: to what power must the base be raised? log10(1000) = 3. In biochemistry, pH = −log10[H+], with [H+] in mol/L. An exponential change has the form y = y0 e^(kt), where e ≈ 2.718. If k is negative, y decays; half-life t1/2 = ln2 ÷ |k| ≈ 0.693 ÷ |k|. Example: [H+] = 2.5 × 10^-5 mol/L gives pH = −log10(2.5 × 10^-5) = 4.60.

sections.heading: Rates and graphs
sections.text: A rate is a change in one quantity per unit change in another, such as µmol of product per minute. On a graph, the slope (gradient) of a straight line is the rate. For an exponential curve, plot ln y against time: a straight line of slope k shows exponential growth or decay. Example: if y = 100 e^(−0.2t), at t = 5, y = 100 × e^(−1) = 36.8. The slope of ln y against t is −0.2 per unit time.

sections.heading: Units and dimensions
sections.text: Every measurement has a unit and a dimension. SI base units include metre (m), kilogram (kg), second (s) and mole (mol). Dimensional analysis checks that both sides of an equation have the same dimensions; it cannot give the numerical factor. Convert by multiplying by ratios equal to one. Example: 0.25 µmol/min = 0.25 × 10^-6 mol ÷ 60 s = 4.17 × 10^-9 mol/s. Carry units through the calculation.

sections.heading: Statistics and uncertainty
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise data. The mean is the sum divided by n; the median is the middle value. Standard deviation (SD) measures spread: s = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)] for a sample. Standard error of the mean (SEM) = s ÷ √n. Example: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 have mean 14, s = √(40 ÷ 4) = 3.16, SEM = 3.16 ÷ √5 = 1.41. A hypothesis test compares a null hypothesis with data. The p-value is the probability of results at least as extreme if the null is true; it is not the probability that the null is true. A t-test compares means. Report uncertainty with units and significant figures.

keyPoints: pH = −log10[H+]; for y = y0 e^(kt), half-life = ln2 ÷ |k| ≈ 0.693 ÷ |k|.
For exponential data, a plot of ln y against time is a straight line with slope k.
Convert units by multiplying by ratios equal to one, and check dimensions on both sides.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample SD = √[Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)]; SEM = s ÷ √n.
The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis is true, not the probability that the null is true.
Report results with units, significant figures and a measure of spread such as SD or SEM.

en.title: Cell biology and biochemical compartmentation
en.short: Covers cell structure, organelles, membranes, transport, cytoskeleton, cell cycle, microscopy and compartmentation.

sections.heading: Cells and organelles
sections.text:
A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out life processes. The plasma membrane encloses the cytoplasm, made of cytosol (fluid) and organelles (specialised structures). Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and organelles such as mitochondria, chloroplasts in plants and algae, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and peroxisomes. Ribosomes build proteins and are not membrane-bound.

Compartmentation means each membrane-bound space has its own enzymes and conditions. Lysosomal enzymes work at acid pH, away from the cytosol. Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and the citric acid cycle in the mitochondrial matrix. Separation lets opposing reactions run at the same time.

sections.heading: Membranes and transport
sections.text:
Membranes are phospholipid bilayers with embedded proteins and are selectively permeable. Small nonpolar molecules such as oxygen diffuse through the lipid. Ions and polar molecules such as glucose need channels or carrier proteins. Osmosis is water movement across a semipermeable membrane from higher to lower water concentration.

Passive transport follows a concentration gradient and needs no ATP. Active transport moves substances against a gradient and uses energy, often ATP; the sodium-potassium pump in animal cells is an example. Endocytosis takes material in by vesicles, and exocytosis releases it. Transport proteins link compartments.

sections.heading: Cytoskeleton and cell cycle
sections.text:
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein filaments. Microtubules, made of tubulin, form tracks and the mitotic spindle. Actin filaments control cell shape and movement. Intermediate filaments give mechanical strength. The cytoskeleton also positions organelles.

The cell cycle runs from one division to the next. Interphase has G1, S and G2; DNA is copied in S. The mitotic phase separates chromosomes and divides the cell. Checkpoints monitor DNA damage and chromosome attachment. The nuclear envelope breaks down during mitosis, so compartments mix temporarily.

sections.heading: Microscopy and case
sections.text: Microscopy shows structure: light microscopes view living cells at about 0.2 micrometre resolution; electron microscopes reveal finer detail in fixed cells. Fluorescence tags molecules. Case: Amaka finds lactate dehydrogenase in cytosol and succinate dehydrogenase on inner mitochondrial membrane, supporting compartmentation.

keyPoints: Compartmentation keeps incompatible reactions in separate membrane-bound spaces.
The plasma membrane is selectively permeable; passive transport needs no ATP, active transport does.
The cytoskeleton gives shape, moves materials and separates chromosomes.
The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S, G2) and mitotic phase, with checkpoints.
Light microscopy resolves about 0.2 micrometre; electron microscopy reveals finer detail.
Lactate dehydrogenase in cytosol and succinate dehydrogenase on inner mitochondrial membrane illustrate compartmentation.

en.title: Amino acids and peptides
en.short: The 20 amino acids, their charge and pKa, ionization, the peptide bond, sequencing and electrophoresis.

sections.heading: The standard set
sections.text: An amino acid has an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain (R group) on the same alpha carbon. The 20 standard amino acids differ only in R. They are grouped as nonpolar, polar uncharged, acidic and basic. Proline is cyclic, with its nitrogen in a ring. 'Essential' means the body cannot make enough; the list varies between species.

sections.heading: Charge and pKa
sections.text: In water the carboxyl group loses a proton (pKa about 2) and the amino group gains one (pKa about 9 to 10), forming a zwitterion with both charges. Side chains ionise too: aspartate and glutamate near pH 4, histidine near 6, cysteine near 8, tyrosine near 10, lysine near 10.5, arginine near 12.5. Values are approximate. Net charge depends on pH. The isoelectric point pI is the pH of zero net charge. For a neutral amino acid, pI = (pKa1 + pKa2) ÷ 2. Glycine: pKa1 2.35, pKa2 9.78, so pI = (2.35 + 9.78) ÷ 2 = 6.07. Below pI it is more positive; above pI, more negative.

sections.heading: The peptide bond
sections.text: A peptide bond joins the alpha-carboxyl of one amino acid to the alpha-amino of the next, losing water. It is planar because the C-N bond has partial double-bond character, so rotation is restricted. Chains are written from the N-terminus (free amino end) to the C-terminus (free carboxyl end). Two cysteines can form a disulfide bond (S-S). Short chains are peptides; long chains are proteins. Hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds.

sections.heading: Sequencing and separation
sections.text: Edman degradation removes and identifies the N-terminal residue one cycle at a time. Trypsin cuts after lysine or arginine; chymotrypsin cuts after aromatic residues. Overlapping fragments give the order. Mass spectrometry is now common. Electrophoresis separates charged molecules in an electric field. At pH 7, glycine (pI 6.07) is nearly neutral and stays near the origin, while lysine (pI 9.74) has net charge about +1 and moves to the cathode. Isoelectric focusing separates by pI.

keyPoints: The 20 standard amino acids share an alpha carbon bearing an amino group, a carboxyl group and a side chain.
In water, amino acids form zwitterions; net charge depends on pH and side-chain pKa values.
pI = (pKa1 + pKa2) ÷ 2 for a neutral amino acid; below pI the net charge is positive, above it negative.
A peptide bond forms by condensation, is planar and runs N-terminus to C-terminus.
Edman degradation and specific protease cuts, with overlapping fragments, give peptide sequence.
Electrophoresis separates amino acids and peptides by charge; isoelectric focusing separates by pI.

en.title: Protein structure and function
en.short: The four levels of protein structure, the forces that hold them, folding, denaturation and domains.

sections.heading: Levels of structure
sections.text: Primary structure is the order of amino acids in a polypeptide chain, joined by peptide bonds. Secondary structure is local folding of the backbone into alpha helices, beta sheets and turns, held by hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups. Tertiary structure is the complete three-dimensional shape of one chain. Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more chains, as in haemoglobin.

sections.heading: Forces and folding
sections.text: Tertiary structure is stabilised by hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds (salt bridges), van der Waals forces and, in some proteins, covalent disulfide bonds between cysteine residues. Hydrophobic side chains tend to cluster inside the folded protein, away from water. Folding is the process by which a chain reaches its native shape. The amino acid sequence usually determines this shape under suitable conditions, but inside cells chaperone proteins help folding and prevent aggregation.

sections.heading: Domains and function
sections.text: A domain is a compact, independently folded part of a chain, often with its own function, such as binding a small molecule. Structure determines function: an enzyme’s active site is a shaped pocket; antibodies bind antigens; channel proteins form pores in membranes. A small change in sequence can alter shape and function. In sickle cell anaemia, a glutamic acid to valine change at position 6 of the beta-globin chain makes haemoglobin HbS prone to polymerise when deoxygenated.

sections.heading: Denaturation
sections.text: Denaturation is loss of the native three-dimensional structure. Heat, extremes of pH, urea, detergents or organic solvents disrupt the weak forces, while peptide bonds remain. Denatured proteins often lose solubility and function. Denaturation may be reversible in some proteins, but in others it is irreversible because the unfolded chain aggregates.

keyPoints: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence; secondary structure is local backbone folding such as alpha helices and beta sheets.
Tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape of one chain; quaternary structure is the assembly of several chains.
Hydrophobic interactions, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, van der Waals forces and disulfide bonds stabilise protein structure.
Folding is guided by sequence and assisted by chaperones; denaturation disrupts weak forces and usually destroys function.
Domains are compact folded regions often associated with specific functions.
A single amino acid change can alter structure and cause disease, as in sickle cell haemoglobin.

en.title: Structure and properties of carbohydrates and lipids
en.short: Monosaccharides, glycosidic bonds, polysaccharides, fatty acids, triacylglycerols, phospholipids and steroids.

sections.heading: Monosaccharides
sections.text:
Monosaccharides are the simplest carbohydrates. Most have the formula (CH2O)n and contain several hydroxyl groups plus an aldehyde or ketone group. Glucose is an aldohexose (six carbons, aldehyde); fructose is a ketohexose. In water they usually form rings.

The many polar hydroxyl groups form hydrogen bonds with water, so monosaccharides are soluble and travel dissolved in body fluids. Their carbonyl group also lets them act as reducing agents.

sections.heading: Glycosidic bonds
sections.text:
Two monosaccharides join by a condensation reaction: one hydroxyl group reacts with another, water is lost, and a glycosidic bond forms. Sucrose (glucose + fructose), lactose (glucose + galactose) and maltose (glucose + glucose) are disaccharides.

Polysaccharides are many units joined this way. Starch and glycogen use α(1→4) links with branches, which pack less tightly and are hydrolysed easily for storage. Cellulose uses β(1→4) links; the alternating orientation gives straight, rigid chains that pack into strong fibres.

sections.heading: Fatty acids and triacylglycerols
sections.text:
Fatty acids are long hydrocarbon chains ending in a carboxyl group. Saturated chains have no double bonds and pack closely. Unsaturated chains have one or more double bonds; the common cis double bond bends the chain, so packing is poorer and melting points are lower.

A triacylglycerol (fat or oil) is glycerol esterified to three fatty acids. It is nonpolar and stores energy without water. Case: olive oil, rich in cis-oleic acid, is liquid at room temperature; butter, rich in saturated fats, is solid.

sections.heading: Phospholipids and steroids
sections.text:
A phospholipid has glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group linked to a small alcohol. The phosphate head is polar and the tails are nonpolar, so the molecule is amphipathic: it forms bilayers in water, the basis of membranes.

Steroids have four fused carbon rings. Cholesterol is a steroid in animal membranes; it stiffens and modulates fluidity and is a precursor of steroid hormones. Plants use related phytosterols. In all these lipids, structure controls solubility, packing and biological role.

keyPoints: Monosaccharides are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones; glucose is an aldohexose and fructose a ketohexose.
A glycosidic bond forms by condensation between two monosaccharides with loss of water.
Starch and glycogen have α(1→4) branched links for storage; cellulose has β(1→4) links for strength.
Saturated fatty acids pack tightly; cis-unsaturated fatty acids kink and lower the melting point.
Triacylglycerols are nonpolar energy stores; phospholipids are amphipathic membrane molecules.
Steroids have four fused rings; cholesterol modulates animal membrane fluidity and is a hormone precursor.

en.title: Nucleic acids: structure and properties
en.short: Nucleotides, DNA base pairing and the double helix, RNA folding, denaturation, hybridisation and supercoiling.

sections.heading: Nucleotides
sections.text: Nucleotides are the building blocks of nucleic acids. Each has a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar and one or more phosphate groups. A base plus sugar without phosphate is a nucleoside. The bases are purines (adenine, guanine) and pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine in DNA, uracil in RNA). DNA uses deoxyribose; RNA uses ribose. Nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds between the 3′ hydroxyl of one sugar and the 5′ phosphate of the next, giving a chain with a 5′ end and a 3′ end.

sections.heading: DNA double helix
sections.text: The DNA double helix has two antiparallel strands wound round a common axis. Bases face inward and pair by hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine (two bonds), guanine with cytosine (three). This complementarity means one strand specifies the other. The sugar-phosphate backbones lie outside. The helix has major and minor grooves.

sections.heading: RNA and folding
sections.text: RNA is usually single-stranded. mRNA carries a protein-coding message; tRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome; rRNA forms part of the ribosome. RNA can fold when complementary stretches within the same molecule pair. This gives stem-loop or hairpin structures. tRNA folds into a cloverleaf in two dimensions and an L shape in three. These folds depend on base pairing and are important for function.

sections.heading: Denaturation and supercoiling
sections.text: Denaturation separates the two DNA strands by breaking hydrogen bonds, usually with heat or alkali; the covalent backbone stays intact. On cooling, complementary strands can anneal, or hybridise. This is the basis of probes, Southern and Northern blotting, and PCR. Hybridisation is specific: more matching bases and higher G+C content give a more stable duplex. Supercoiling is the coiling of an already coiled DNA molecule. In cells DNA is usually negatively supercoiled. Topoisomerases change the linking number by cutting and rejoining DNA.

keyPoints: Nucleotide = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate; DNA uses deoxyribose and thymine, RNA uses ribose and uracil.
DNA strands are antiparallel and pair A with T by two hydrogen bonds and G with C by three.
RNA is usually single-stranded but folds into stem-loops; mRNA, tRNA and rRNA have distinct roles.
Denaturation breaks hydrogen bonds and separates strands; hybridisation lets complementary strands anneal.
Supercoiling is coiling of an already coiled DNA molecule, and topoisomerases change the linking number.
Higher G+C content gives a more stable duplex and a higher melting temperature.

en.title: Enzymes: kinetics, inhibition and regulation
en.short: Enzyme classes, active sites, Michaelis-Menten kinetics, inhibition, allosteric control and activity factors.

sections.heading: Classification and active sites
sections.text: Enzymes are classified by the reaction they catalyse into seven EC classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases and translocases. Each enzyme has an EC number. The active site is the pocket where substrate binds and catalysis occurs. It is formed by residues brought together by folding, and binding may involve induced fit. Cofactors and coenzymes are non-protein helpers; metal ions are common cofactors.

sections.heading: Michaelis-Menten kinetics
sections.text:
For a single-substrate enzyme, v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]). Vmax is the limiting rate at saturating substrate. Km is the substrate concentration giving v = Vmax ÷ 2. In the simple model, Km = (k−1 + k2) ÷ k1, so it is only an inverse measure of affinity when k2 is small. kcat = Vmax ÷ [E]total is the turnover number.

Taking reciprocals gives 1/v = (Km ÷ Vmax)(1 ÷ [S]) + 1 ÷ Vmax. A Lineweaver-Burk plot of 1/v against 1/[S] is a straight line with y-intercept 1 ÷ Vmax and x-intercept −1 ÷ Km.

Example: Vmax = 100 µmol/min and Km = 5 mM. At [S] = 20 mM, v = 100 × 20 ÷ (5 + 20) = 80 µmol/min. Then 1/v = 0.0125 min/µmol and 1/[S] = 0.05 mM−1. The line is 1/v = 0.05(1/[S]) + 0.01.

sections.heading: Reversible inhibition
sections.text: Reversible inhibitors bind non-covalently. A competitive inhibitor binds free enzyme, raising apparent Km but leaving Vmax unchanged. An uncompetitive inhibitor binds ES only, lowering both apparent Km and Vmax. A pure non-competitive inhibitor binds E and ES equally, lowering Vmax but leaving Km unchanged. Mixed inhibition changes both. On Lineweaver-Burk plots, competitive lines meet at the y-axis, non-competitive lines at the x-axis, and uncompetitive lines are parallel.

sections.heading: Allosteric regulation
sections.text: Allosteric enzymes have regulatory sites away from the active site; effectors change activity and often give S-shaped kinetics, so simple Km and Vmax do not apply. Activity also depends on pH, temperature, substrate and enzyme concentration, cofactors and inhibitors; high temperature or extreme pH denatures enzymes.

keyPoints: Enzymes fall into seven EC classes: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases and translocases.
Michaelis-Menten equation: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]); Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax.
Lineweaver-Burk equation: 1/v = (Km ÷ Vmax)(1 ÷ [S]) + 1 ÷ Vmax; y-intercept = 1 ÷ Vmax, x-intercept = −1 ÷ Km.
Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km with unchanged Vmax; pure non-competitive inhibition lowers Vmax with unchanged Km; uncompetitive inhibition lowers both.
Allosteric effectors bind regulatory sites and often produce sigmoidal kinetics.
Enzyme activity depends on pH, temperature, substrate and enzyme concentration, cofactors and inhibitors; extremes denature the enzyme.

en.title: Bioenergetics: thermodynamics and ATP
en.short: Free energy, coupled reactions, ATP hydrolysis, phosphorylation potential and redox energy.

sections.heading: Free energy
sections.text:
At constant temperature and pressure, the Gibbs free energy change decides direction: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. Enthalpy ΔH is heat exchanged at constant pressure. Entropy ΔS measures dispersal of energy and matter. A negative ΔG means the reaction is spontaneous as written; positive means it needs work; zero means equilibrium.

Standard biochemical values, written ΔG°′, refer to pH 7, 298 K and defined concentrations. Actual ΔG depends on concentrations: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient.

sections.heading: Coupled reactions
sections.text:
Coupled reactions link an exergonic step to an endergonic one through a shared intermediate, so the overall ΔG is the sum of the steps. If the sum is negative, the pair proceeds.

For example, phosphorylation of glucose is unfavourable alone, but coupling to ATP hydrolysis makes the overall reaction favourable. Enzymes lower activation energy; they do not change ΔG.

sections.heading: ATP and phosphorylation potential
sections.text:
ATP hydrolysis, ATP + H2O -> ADP + Pi (inorganic phosphate), has a standard biochemical ΔG°′ of about −30.5 kJ/mol. The phosphorylation potential is the actual ΔG under cellular conditions: ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln([ADP][Pi]/[ATP]). Some texts quote the ratio [ATP]/([ADP][Pi]) instead.

Example at 298 K with Q = 0.01: RT = 8.314 × 298 ÷ 1000 = 2.48 kJ/mol; ln 0.01 = −4.605; ΔG = −30.5 + (2.48 × −4.605) = −41.9 kJ/mol. Cellular values vary.

sections.heading: Redox and energy carriers
sections.text:
Reduction potential E°′ measures a couple’s tendency to accept electrons. For a redox reaction, ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′, where n is electrons transferred, F is 96,485 C/mol and ΔE°′ = E°′ acceptor − E°′ donor. Electrons flow from the lower to the higher E°′.

High-energy compounds are those with large negative hydrolysis ΔG, such as ATP (phosphoanhydride bonds), phosphocreatine, phosphoenolpyruvate and thioesters like acetyl-CoA. The term describes free energy release, not literal bond strength.

keyPoints: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; negative ΔG means spontaneous at constant T and P.
Actual free energy is ΔG = ΔG°′ + RT ln Q.
Coupled reactions add their ΔG values; an exergonic step can drive an endergonic one.
ATP hydrolysis has ΔG°′ about −30.5 kJ/mol; phosphorylation potential is its actual ΔG.
Redox free energy is ΔG°′ = −nFΔE°′, with electrons flowing to the higher E°′.
High-energy compounds release much free energy on hydrolysis; the label is not about bond strength.

en.title: Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis: opposing pathways
en.short: Glycolysis reactions, regulation, fermentation, and gluconeogenesis with hormonal control.

sections.heading: Glycolysis reactions
sections.text: Glycolysis is the ten-step breakdown of one glucose molecule to two pyruvate molecules in the cytosol. The first five steps invest two ATP: hexokinase (glucokinase in liver) phosphorylates glucose, and phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) phosphorylates fructose-6-phosphate. The six-carbon sugar is then split into two three-carbon molecules. The last five steps recover energy. Two steps make ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, meaning a phosphate group is transferred from a high-energy substrate to ADP without oxygen. Net yield per glucose: 2 ATP (4 made minus 2 used), 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate.

sections.heading: Regulation and fermentation
sections.text: PFK-1 is the main control point. ATP and citrate inhibit it; AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activate it. Hexokinase (but not glucokinase) is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate, and pyruvate kinase by ATP. When oxygen is scarce, NADH cannot be reoxidised by the electron transport chain, so fermentation reduces pyruvate to lactate (animals and some bacteria) or to ethanol and CO2 (yeast). This regenerates NAD+, allowing glycolysis to continue. Fermentation adds no ATP beyond the net 2 ATP of glycolysis.

sections.heading: Gluconeogenesis and hormones
sections.text: Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from lactate, glycerol and amino acids, mainly in liver and kidney cortex. It bypasses the three irreversible glycolytic steps using four enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase makes oxaloacetate; phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase makes phosphoenolpyruvate; fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase makes fructose-6-phosphate; and glucose-6-phosphatase releases free glucose. Two pyruvate to one glucose costs 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH. Insulin stimulates glycolysis and inhibits gluconeogenesis. Glucagon raises liver cAMP, activating gluconeogenesis and slowing glycolysis; adrenaline and cortisol also support glucose production. Example: one glucose gives net 2 ATP, but reversing it costs 6 high-energy phosphate bonds (4 ATP plus 2 GTP) and 2 NADH, so the pathways are controlled reciprocally.

keyPoints: Glycolysis converts one glucose to two pyruvate with net 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
Substrate-level phosphorylation makes ATP by transferring phosphate from a high-energy substrate to ADP.
PFK-1 is the main regulated enzyme of glycolysis, inhibited by ATP and citrate and activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate.
Fermentation regenerates NAD+ by reducing pyruvate to lactate or ethanol, allowing glycolysis to continue without oxygen.
Gluconeogenesis bypasses the three irreversible glycolytic steps using four enzymes: pyruvate carboxylase, PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase and glucose-6-phosphatase.
Insulin stimulates glycolysis and inhibits gluconeogenesis, while glucagon does the opposite.

en.title: The citric acid cycle
en.short: Acetyl-CoA formation, the eight cycle reactions, energy and biosynthesis roles, and regulation.

sections.heading: Acetyl-CoA formation
sections.text: Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by oxidative decarboxylation: pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ gives acetyl-CoA + CO2 + NADH. This irreversible step links glycolysis to the cycle. Acetyl-CoA also comes from fatty acid β-oxidation and amino acid breakdown. Coenzyme A carries the two-carbon acetyl group.

sections.heading: The cycle reactions
sections.text: Acetyl-CoA (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C), catalysed by citrate synthase. Aconitase isomerises citrate to isocitrate. Isocitrate dehydrogenase decarboxylates and oxidises it to α-ketoglutarate, producing NADH and CO2. α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase does the same to succinyl-CoA, producing NADH and CO2. Succinyl-CoA synthetase converts succinyl-CoA to succinate, making GTP. Succinate dehydrogenase oxidises succinate to fumarate, producing FADH2. Fumarase hydrates fumarate to malate. Malate dehydrogenase oxidises malate to oxaloacetate, producing NADH. One turn returns oxaloacetate.

sections.heading: Oxidation and biosynthesis
sections.text: Each turn oxidises one acetyl group to two CO2, conserving energy as 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP. The NADH and FADH2 feed oxidative phosphorylation. Using P/O ratios of 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2, ATP equivalent = 3×2.5 + 1×1.5 + 1 = 10 per acetyl-CoA. Older texts use 3 and 2, giving 12. The cycle itself uses no O2, but it stops without O2 because NADH cannot be reoxidised. The cycle is amphibolic: it oxidises fuel and supplies precursors. Oxaloacetate feeds gluconeogenesis, α-ketoglutarate feeds glutamate, succinyl-CoA feeds haem, and citrate feeds fatty acid synthesis. Anaplerotic reactions such as pyruvate carboxylase replenish oxaloacetate.

sections.heading: Regulation
sections.text: The cycle is controlled at its irreversible steps. Citrate synthase is inhibited by ATP, NADH and succinyl-CoA. Isocitrate dehydrogenase is activated by ADP and Ca²⁺, and inhibited by ATP and NADH. α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase is inhibited by succinyl-CoA and NADH. Pyruvate dehydrogenase is inhibited by ATP, NADH and acetyl-CoA, and activated by ADP and pyruvate. A high energy charge (ATP, NADH) slows the cycle; a low energy charge (ADP, AMP) speeds it. This matches oxidation to demand.

keyPoints: Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, CO2 and NADH in an irreversible oxidative decarboxylation.
One turn of the cycle: acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate gives citrate, then two decarboxylations release 2 CO2 and regenerate oxaloacetate.
Each turn yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP; with P/O ratios 2.5 and 1.5 the ATP equivalent is 3×2.5 + 1×1.5 + 1 = 10.
The cycle is amphibolic: it oxidises acetyl groups and supplies precursors for gluconeogenesis, amino acids, haem and fatty acids.
Anaplerotic reactions, such as pyruvate carboxylase, replenish oxaloacetate.
Regulation at citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase matches cycle rate to ATP demand.

en.title: Oxidative phosphorylation and the electron transport chain
en.short: The respiratory chain, proton gradient, ATP synthase, oxygen use, uncoupling and inhibitors.

sections.heading: Electron transport chain
sections.text: The electron transport chain (ETC) is a set of complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase) accepts electrons from NADH. Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) accepts them from FADH2 and does not pump protons. Complexes III (cytochrome bc1) and IV (cytochrome c oxidase) pass electrons on. Ubiquinone (CoQ) carries electrons from I or II to III, and cytochrome c carries them from III to IV. The redox energy pumps H+ from the matrix to the intermembrane space.

sections.heading: Chemiosmotic coupling
sections.text:
The pumped protons create a proton motive force (PMF), from a pH difference and a charge difference. Chemiosmotic coupling means the ETC and ATP synthesis are linked by this gradient, not by a direct chemical intermediate. Oxygen is the terminal electron acceptor at Complex IV, where it is reduced to water. Without oxygen, the chain backs up and the gradient falls.

Example: NADH + H+ + 0.5 O2 → NAD+ + H2O. E°' is −0.320 V for NAD+/NADH and +0.816 V for O2/H2O. ΔE°' = 1.136 V. ΔG°' = −nFΔE°' = −2 × 96,485 × 1.136 = −219 kJ/mol.

sections.heading: ATP synthase
sections.text: ATP synthase (Complex V) is a rotary motor. Protons flow back into the matrix through its Fo channel, and this rotation drives the F1 head, which joins ADP and Pi (inorganic phosphate) to make ATP. Oxidative phosphorylation is electron transport plus this ATP synthesis. Commonly quoted yields are about 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2, but exact values vary with shuttle systems and conventions.

sections.heading: Uncoupling and inhibition
sections.text: An uncoupler carries protons across the inner membrane, letting them leak back without ATP synthase. Electron transport continues, the gradient falls, and energy becomes heat. UCP1 (thermogenin) does this in brown fat; 2,4-dinitrophenol is an example. Inhibitors act specifically: rotenone at Complex I, malonate at Complex II, antimycin A at Complex III, cyanide and carbon monoxide at Complex IV, and oligomycin at ATP synthase. Blocking the chain lowers the gradient; blocking ATP synthase raises it and slows the chain.

keyPoints: The ETC passes electrons from NADH and FADH2 through Complexes I to IV to oxygen, the terminal acceptor, which becomes water.
Complexes I, III and IV pump H+; Complex II does not.
Ubiquinone and cytochrome c are mobile electron carriers.
The proton motive force links electron transport to ATP synthase, a rotary enzyme.
Uncouplers dissipate the gradient as heat; specific inhibitors block complexes or ATP synthase.
For NADH oxidation by oxygen, ΔG°' = −nFΔE°' = −219 kJ/mol using E°' values −0.320 V and +0.816 V.

en.title: Photosynthesis and carbon fixation
en.short: Light reactions, photosystems, photophosphorylation, the Calvin cycle and C3, C4, CAM and microbial fixation.

sections.heading: Light reactions
sections.text:
Photosynthesis begins in the thylakoid membrane. A photosystem is a pigment-protein complex that absorbs light and passes excited electrons to an acceptor. Photosystem II (PSII, P680) oxidises water through the oxygen-evolving complex, releasing O2 and electrons. These electrons travel via plastoquinone, the cytochrome b6f complex and plastocyanin to photosystem I (PSI, P700), then via ferredoxin to NADP+ reductase, forming NADPH.

Electron transfer pumps protons into the thylakoid lumen. The proton gradient drives ATP synthase. This light-driven ATP synthesis is photophosphorylation. Noncyclic electron flow makes ATP and NADPH; cyclic flow around PSI makes ATP only.

sections.heading: Calvin cycle
sections.text:
The Calvin cycle, or reductive pentose phosphate pathway, fixes CO2 in the stroma. RuBisCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) adds CO2 to ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP), giving two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate. ATP and NADPH reduce these to triose phosphates. Most triose phosphate regenerates RuBP; some leaves as sugar or storage product.

Stoichiometry: per CO2 fixed, the cycle uses 3 ATP and 2 NADPH. For one glucose (6 CO2): 6 × 3 = 18 ATP and 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH. RuBisCO also reacts with O2 in photorespiration, which wastes carbon and energy.

sections.heading: Plant fixation routes
sections.text:
C3 plants fix CO2 directly by the Calvin cycle in mesophyll cells. C4 plants first fix CO2 as bicarbonate using PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells, forming a four-carbon acid. This acid moves to bundle-sheath cells, where decarboxylation releases CO2 for the Calvin cycle. C4 reduces photorespiration but costs extra ATP.

CAM plants separate the steps in time: they fix CO2 at night into malate, then release it by day for the Calvin cycle. This saves water in dry habitats. C3, C4 and CAM are adaptations, not strict taxonomic groups.

sections.heading: Microbial routes
sections.text: Many autotrophic bacteria use the Calvin cycle. Others, including many archaea, use the reductive acetyl-CoA (Wood-Ljungdahl) pathway, the reductive tricarboxylic acid cycle, or the 3-hydroxypropionate bicycle. These pathways differ in ATP cost and oxygen sensitivity. Anoxygenic phototrophs often use cyclic photophosphorylation and may fix carbon by one of these routes.

keyPoints: PSII (P680) splits water, releasing O2, and passes electrons to PSI (P700), which reduces NADP+ to NADPH.
Proton pumping during electron transport drives ATP synthase; this is photophosphorylation, and cyclic flow makes ATP without NADPH.
The Calvin cycle fixes CO2 using RuBisCO and consumes 3 ATP and 2 NADPH per CO2.
For one glucose, Calvin fixation uses 6 × 3 = 18 ATP and 6 × 2 = 12 NADPH.
C4 plants use PEP carboxylase and bundle-sheath decarboxylation; CAM plants fix CO2 at night and run the Calvin cycle by day.
Microbes fix carbon by the Calvin cycle, Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, reductive TCA cycle or 3-hydroxypropionate bicycle.

en.title: Glycogen metabolism and the pentose phosphate pathway
en.short: Glycogen synthesis and breakdown, enzyme control, and the pentose phosphate pathway making NADPH.

sections.heading: Glycogen synthesis
sections.text: Glycogen is a branched polymer of glucose. Most links are alpha-1,4; branch points are alpha-1,6. It is stored mainly in liver and skeletal muscle. Synthesis starts with glucose-6-phosphate, which phosphoglucomutase converts to glucose-1-phosphate. UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase then makes UDP-glucose from glucose-1-phosphate and UTP. Glycogenin, a protein primer, accepts the first glucose. Glycogen synthase extends chains at non-reducing ends by alpha-1,4 links, and branching enzyme moves a block to make an alpha-1,6 branch. Adding one glucose from glucose-6-phosphate costs one UTP; starting from free glucose also costs one ATP, so two ATP equivalents in total.

sections.heading: Breakdown and control
sections.text: Glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose units from non-reducing ends using inorganic phosphate, giving glucose-1-phosphate, not free glucose. Debranching enzyme handles alpha-1,6 points. Liver has glucose-6-phosphatase and can release glucose into blood; muscle lacks it and uses glucose-6-phosphate for glycolysis. Phosphorylase is controlled covalently and allosterically. Phosphorylation by phosphorylase kinase converts less active b to active a. In muscle, AMP activates b and ATP or glucose-6-phosphate inhibits. In liver, glucose inhibits a. Glycogen synthase is active when dephosphorylated. Glucose-6-phosphate activates it allosterically; phosphorylation by PKA and GSK3 inactivates it. Insulin promotes dephosphorylation through protein phosphatase 1, so synthesis and breakdown are reciprocally controlled.

sections.heading: Pentose phosphate pathway
sections.text: The pentose phosphate pathway has an oxidative phase and a nonoxidative phase. In the oxidative phase, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (rate-limiting, inhibited by NADPH) makes 6-phosphogluconolactone, which is hydrolysed to 6-phosphogluconate. 6-Phosphogluconate dehydrogenase then decarboxylates it to ribulose-5-phosphate, producing two NADPH and one CO2 per glucose-6-phosphate. Ribulose-5-phosphate is isomerised to ribose-5-phosphate, needed for nucleotides. Transketolase and transaldolase then convert pentose phosphates into fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, which can rejoin glycolysis. NADPH is the reducing power for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis and keeps glutathione reduced in red blood cells. It does not make ATP directly. Worked example: three glucose-6-phosphate can give two fructose-6-phosphate, one glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, three CO2 and six NADPH.

keyPoints: Glycogen synthase adds glucose from UDP-glucose to non-reducing ends, making alpha-1,4 links; branching enzyme makes alpha-1,6 branches.
Glycogen phosphorylase uses inorganic phosphate to release glucose-1-phosphate; debranching enzyme handles alpha-1,6 points.
Phosphorylase is activated by phosphorylation (b to a) and by AMP in muscle; ATP and glucose-6-phosphate oppose activation, and liver glucose inhibits the a form.
Glycogen synthase is active when dephosphorylated; glucose-6-phosphate activates it and insulin promotes its dephosphorylation.
Oxidative pentose phosphate pathway: glucose-6-phosphate + 2 NADP+ + H2O gives ribulose-5-phosphate + 2 NADPH + CO2; glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is rate-limiting.
Three glucose-6-phosphate can give 2 fructose-6-phosphate + 1 glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate + 3 CO2 + 6 NADPH, and NADPH supplies reducing power for biosynthesis and glutathione regeneration.

en.title: Lipid metabolism: oxidation, synthesis and cholesterol
en.short: Fatty acid oxidation and synthesis, ketone bodies, complex lipids and cholesterol.

sections.heading: Fatty acid oxidation
sections.text:
Activation joins a fatty acid to coenzyme A: fatty acid + CoA + ATP gives acyl-CoA + AMP + PPi, catalysed by acyl-CoA synthetase. This costs two ATP equivalents. The carnitine shuttle carries long-chain acyl-CoA into the mitochondrial matrix.

Beta-oxidation removes two carbons per cycle as acetyl-CoA. Each cycle yields one FADH2, one NADH and one acetyl-CoA through dehydrogenation, hydration and thiolase steps.

Example: palmitate (C16:0) gives 7 cycles and 8 acetyl-CoA. With NADH about 2.5 ATP, FADH2 about 1.5 ATP and acetyl-CoA about 10 ATP:
7 × 1.5 + 7 × 2.5 + 8 × 10 − 2 = 106 ATP
Older texts using 2 and 3 give 129 ATP.

sections.heading: Ketone bodies
sections.text: Ketone bodies are acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. The liver makes them from acetyl-CoA when oxaloacetate is low, as in fasting or uncontrolled diabetes. HMG-CoA synthase and HMG-CoA lyase are key enzymes. The liver lacks thiophorase, so it cannot use them; extrahepatic tissues convert them back to acetyl-CoA. Excessive production causes ketoacidosis because acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate are acids.

sections.heading: Fatty acid synthesis
sections.text: Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytosol. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA from acetyl-CoA, CO2 and ATP; this is the committed step. Fatty acid synthase then adds two carbons per cycle using NADPH, releasing CO2, and usually stops at palmitate (C16:0). Acetyl-CoA reaches the cytosol via citrate. Synthesis uses malonyl-CoA, NADPH and acyl carrier protein; beta-oxidation uses CoA, FAD and NAD+ in mitochondria. Insulin promotes synthesis; glucagon promotes oxidation.

sections.heading: Complex lipids and cholesterol
sections.text:
Triacylglycerol is made from glycerol-3-phosphate and acyl-CoA via phosphatidic acid and diacylglycerol. Phospholipids form from phosphatidic acid or diacylglycerol and a head group; phospholipases hydrolyse them. Lipolysis releases fatty acids from triacylglycerol.

Cholesterol is synthesised from acetyl-CoA in the cytosol and endoplasmic reticulum, mainly in the liver. HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme and the target of statins. Cholesterol is a precursor of bile acids, steroid hormones and vitamin D. Lipoproteins transport lipids: chylomicrons, VLDL, LDL and HDL.

keyPoints: Fatty acid activation forms acyl-CoA and costs two ATP equivalents.
Each beta-oxidation cycle removes one acetyl-CoA and yields one FADH2 and one NADH.
Palmitate yields 106 ATP with modern P/O ratios: 7 × 1.5 + 7 × 2.5 + 8 × 10 − 2 = 106.
Ketone bodies are acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetone; the liver makes them but cannot use them.
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase makes malonyl-CoA, the committed step of fatty acid synthesis.
HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis and the target of statins.

en.title: Nitrogen metabolism: amino acids and nucleotides
en.short: Amino acid catabolism, the urea cycle, nucleotide synthesis and breakdown, and related disorders.

sections.heading: Amino acid catabolism
sections.text: Most amino acids are catabolised in the liver. The first step removes the α-amino group. In transamination, an aminotransferase transfers it to α-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate and an α-keto acid. Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP), a vitamin B6 derivative, is the cofactor. Glutamate then undergoes oxidative deamination by glutamate dehydrogenase, releasing ammonia (NH3, mostly present as NH4+) and regenerating α-ketoglutarate. Ammonia is toxic, so blood carries it mainly as glutamine and alanine. Carbon skeletons enter the citric acid cycle or feed gluconeogenesis or ketogenesis; amino acids may be glucogenic, ketogenic or both.

sections.heading: The urea cycle
sections.text: Ammonia is converted to urea in the liver. Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) condenses ammonia and bicarbonate in mitochondria; N-acetylglutamate activates it. Ornithine transcarbamoylase forms citrulline. Argininosuccinate synthetase adds aspartate, the second nitrogen, and argininosuccinate lyase releases fumarate. Arginase splits arginine into urea and ornithine, which re-enters the cycle. Fumarate links the cycle to the citric acid cycle. Example: urea (CH4N2O) has molar mass 60 g/mol and 28 g nitrogen per mole. Excreting 30 g urea removes 30 × 28 ÷ 60 = 14 g nitrogen.

sections.heading: Nucleotide turnover
sections.text: Purine nucleotides are built de novo on a ribose-5-phosphate scaffold supplied by phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP); the purine ring is assembled stepwise. Pyrimidine nucleotides are made as orotate first, then attached to PRPP. Salvage pathways reuse free bases: hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) salvages hypoxanthine and guanine, and adenine phosphoribosyltransferase (APRT) salvages adenine. In humans, purine catabolism ends in uric acid, which is poorly soluble. Pyrimidine catabolism gives soluble products such as β-alanine and β-aminoisobutyrate.

sections.heading: Disorders
sections.text: Disorders arise when an enzyme or transporter fails. Phenylketonuria (phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency) causes phenylalanine accumulation; treatment is a low-phenylalanine diet, and newborn screening differs by country. Maple syrup urine disease affects branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase. Alkaptonuria is homogentisate oxidase deficiency. Urea cycle disorders, such as ornithine transcarbamoylase deficiency, cause hyperammonaemia (high blood ammonia). Gout results from urate crystal deposition in joints. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is HGPRT deficiency, with hyperuricaemia (high blood urate) and neurological problems. Check current local guidelines.

keyPoints: Transamination transfers an amino group to α-ketoglutarate, forming glutamate; PLP is the cofactor.
Glutamate dehydrogenase releases ammonia by oxidative deamination.
The urea cycle uses ammonia and aspartate as nitrogen sources and links to the citric acid cycle through fumarate.
Urea contains 28 g nitrogen per 60 g, so nitrogen removed = urea mass × 28 ÷ 60.
Purines are built on PRPP and degraded to uric acid in humans; pyrimidines are made as orotate and degraded to soluble products.
HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan syndrome; urea cycle defects and phenylketonuria are important inherited disorders.

en.title: DNA replication and repair
en.short: Semiconservative replication, polymerases and proofreading, telomeres, and the main DNA repair pathways.

sections.heading: Replication fork
sections.text: DNA replication is semiconservative: each parent strand is a template for a new strand. E. coli replication starts at one origin and proceeds bidirectionally; eukaryotes use many origins. Helicase unwinds the helix and single-strand binding proteins hold the strands apart. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only to a free 3′ hydroxyl group, so synthesis runs 5′ to 3′. The leading strand is made continuously. The lagging strand is made as short Okazaki fragments, each begun by an RNA primer made by primase. DNA ligase joins the fragments after the RNA is removed.

sections.heading: Polymerases and proofreading
sections.text: In Escherichia coli, DNA polymerase III is the main replicative enzyme; polymerase I removes RNA primers and fills the gaps. Eukaryotes use polymerase α for priming, polymerase δ for lagging-strand synthesis and polymerase ε for leading-strand synthesis. Replicative polymerases have 3′ to 5′ exonuclease activity, which proofreads: a wrong nucleotide is removed before synthesis continues. This lowers the error rate. After replication, mismatch repair corrects errors that escape proofreading.

sections.heading: Telomeres
sections.text: Linear chromosomes shorten at each round of replication because the lagging strand cannot copy the end. Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences at the ends that protect the chromosome. In humans the repeat is TTAGGG. Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase (an enzyme that copies RNA into DNA) carrying its own RNA template, extends the telomere in germ cells, stem cells and many cancer cells. Most somatic cells have little telomerase, so telomeres shorten with cell divisions.

sections.heading: Repair pathways
sections.text: DNA repair counters damage. Direct reversal removes some lesions without cutting the DNA. Base excision repair removes a damaged base and replaces it. Nucleotide excision repair removes a short stretch around a bulky lesion, such as a pyrimidine dimer caused by ultraviolet light. Mismatch repair corrects replication errors. Double-strand breaks are repaired by homologous recombination, which uses a sister chromatid as template, or by non-homologous end joining, which joins broken ends and can lose bases. Inherited faults in mismatch repair cause Lynch syndrome, a cancer predisposition.

keyPoints: DNA replication is semiconservative and synthesis is always 5′ to 3′.
The leading strand is continuous; the lagging strand is made as Okazaki fragments.
DNA polymerase III is the main bacterial replicase; eukaryotic priming uses polymerase α, with δ and ε for lagging and leading strands.
Proofreading by 3′ to 5′ exonuclease and mismatch repair reduce replication errors.
Telomerase extends telomeres in germ cells, stem cells and many cancer cells; most somatic cells lack it.
Main repair pathways include direct reversal, base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair, mismatch repair, homologous recombination and non-homologous end joining.

en.title: Transcription and RNA processing
en.short: RNA polymerase, promoters, prokaryotic and eukaryotic transcription, capping, polyadenylation and splicing.

sections.heading: RNA polymerase and promoters
sections.text: RNA polymerase (RNA pol) is the enzyme that makes RNA from a DNA template. It copies the template strand 3' to 5' and builds RNA 5' to 3', adding nucleotides to the 3' end. A promoter is the DNA sequence where RNA pol binds and starts. In bacteria, the sigma factor helps RNA pol recognise promoters such as the −10 and −35 elements. In eukaryotes, RNA pol II needs general transcription factors (for example TFIID, which binds the TATA box) to form the pre-initiation complex.

sections.heading: Prokaryotes and eukaryotes
sections.text: Bacteria have one main RNA polymerase. Transcription and translation can occur together, and the primary transcript is usually the mRNA; bacterial genes are often in operons and usually lack introns. Eukaryotes have three nuclear RNA polymerases: pol I makes rRNA, pol II makes mRNA, pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA. Pol II transcription is separate from translation, occurs in the nucleus, and produces a pre-mRNA that must be processed. Specific transcription factors and enhancers regulate eukaryotic genes.

sections.heading: Capping and polyadenylation
sections.text: The 5' cap is a 7-methylguanosine joined to the first nucleotide by a 5'-to-5' triphosphate link. It protects the RNA end, helps export from the nucleus and helps ribosomes bind. Polyadenylation: a poly(A) signal (AAUAAA in many eukaryotes) directs cleavage of the pre-mRNA about 10 to 30 nucleotides downstream, then poly(A) polymerase adds a poly(A) tail, commonly about 50 to 250 adenine residues in mammals; the length varies.

sections.heading: Splicing and example
sections.text: Splicing removes introns (intervening sequences) and joins exons (the sequences kept in the mature RNA). The spliceosome, made of small nuclear RNAs and proteins, recognises the 5' GU and 3' AG splice sites and a branch-point A. Two transesterification steps (bond exchanges) cut the intron as a lariat and ligate the exons. Alternative splicing can produce different mRNAs from one gene. Example: a 5,000-nucleotide pre-mRNA has introns of 800, 1,200 and 500 nucleotides. Splicing removes 2,500 nucleotides, leaving 2,500; adding a 200-adenine tail gives about 2,700 nucleotides.

keyPoints: RNA polymerase makes RNA 5' to 3' from the DNA template strand.
Bacterial RNA polymerase uses sigma factor to recognise −10 and −35 promoter elements, while eukaryotic RNA pol II uses general transcription factors at the TATA box.
Eukaryotes have three nuclear RNA polymerases: pol I for rRNA, pol II for mRNA, pol III for tRNA and 5S rRNA.
The 5' cap is 7-methylguanosine joined by a 5'-to-5' triphosphate link and helps protect, export and translate the RNA.
Polyadenylation depends on a poly(A) signal, cleavage downstream, and addition of a poly(A) tail whose length varies.
The spliceosome removes introns as lariat intermediates and joins exons; alternative splicing can make different mRNAs from one gene.

en.title: Translation and protein synthesis
en.short: The genetic code, ribosomes, tRNA charging, the three stages of translation and post-translational modification.

sections.heading: The genetic code
sections.text:
The genetic code maps each mRNA codon, a triplet read 5' to 3', to an amino acid. Of 64 codons, 61 specify amino acids and three (UAA, UAG, UGA) stop. AUG is methionine and the usual start. The code is degenerate, non-overlapping and read in one frame. Wobble allows one tRNA to read codons differing at the third base. It is nearly universal, with exceptions in mitochondria.

Example: 5'-AUG GCU UUU UAA-3' gives Met-Ala-Phe and stop.

sections.heading: tRNA charging
sections.text: Each tRNA is an adaptor. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge it in two steps: activation with ATP to aminoacyl-AMP (releasing pyrophosphate), then transfer to the terminal adenosine of the tRNA’s CCA end. The enzyme must select both the correct amino acid and tRNA, the second genetic code. Proofreading corrects errors. Charging costs two high-energy bonds.

sections.heading: Ribosome and the stages
sections.text: The ribosome has a large and small subunit (70S = 50S + 30S in bacteria; 80S = 60S + 40S in eukaryotes) and A, P and E sites. Initiation: the small subunit binds mRNA and initiator tRNA (fMet in bacteria, Met in eukaryotes); the large subunit joins. Bacteria use the Shine-Dalgarno sequence, eukaryotes the 5' cap and Kozak sequence. Elongation repeats: a charged tRNA enters the A site with GTP and EF-Tu (EF-1A); peptidyl transferase, a ribozyme in the large subunit, forms the peptide bond; translocation by EF-G (EF-2) and GTP moves tRNAs. Termination: a stop codon enters the A site, a release factor binds, and the chain is released.

sections.heading: After the chain
sections.text: New chains fold, often with chaperones. Post-translational modification changes them: cleavage (signal peptides; proinsulin to insulin), glycosylation, phosphorylation, hydroxylation (proline in collagen), acetylation, lipidation and disulfide bonds. These set activity, location and lifetime.

keyPoints: The code is read in triplets: 61 sense codons, three stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA), and AUG starts and codes methionine.
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNA with the correct amino acid using ATP, forming an ester bond at the CCA end.
The ribosome has A, P and E sites; peptidyl transferase is a ribozyme in the large subunit.
Initiation differs: bacteria use Shine-Dalgarno and fMet; eukaryotes use the cap, Kozak sequence and Met.
Each residue added costs about four high-energy bonds: two for charging, one for delivery and one for translocation.
Post-translational modification (cleavage, glycosylation, phosphorylation and others) determines a protein’s final activity and location.

en.title: Gene regulation and epigenetics
en.short: Operons, transcription factors, chromatin changes, epigenetic marks and RNA-based control.

sections.heading: Operons
sections.text:
An operon is a set of genes in bacteria or archaea transcribed together from one promoter, plus the DNA elements that control them. The lac operon of Escherichia coli is the standard example.

When lactose is present and glucose is low, the repressor LacI leaves the operator, and the CAP-cAMP complex helps RNA polymerase bind. The genes for lactose uptake and cleavage are then expressed. When glucose is high, CAP-cAMP is scarce, so expression stays low even with lactose. This is positive and negative control together.

sections.heading: Transcription factors
sections.text:
Transcription factors are proteins that bind specific DNA sequences and increase or decrease transcription. Activators bind promoters or distant control sequences called enhancers and recruit RNA polymerase or coactivators; repressors block activation.

In eukaryotes, many factors act together on one gene, so control is combinatorial. A gene may respond to several signals. Hormone receptors are one example: a steroid hormone binds its receptor, and the receptor then acts as a transcription factor.

sections.heading: Chromatin and epigenetics
sections.text:
DNA in eukaryotes is wrapped around histone proteins to form chromatin. Chromatin remodelling complexes move or eject DNA-protein packages called nucleosomes. Histone acetyltransferases add acetyl groups, usually loosening chromatin, while deacetylases tighten it. Histone methylation can activate or repress, depending on the residue.

DNA methylation at CpG sites (cytosine next to guanine) usually represses transcription in mammals. Such marks are epigenetic: they alter expression without changing DNA sequence, and some are copied through cell division. X-chromosome inactivation in female mammals is an example.

sections.heading: RNA-based control
sections.text:
RNA also regulates gene expression. MicroRNAs are short RNAs that base-pair with target mRNAs and reduce translation or promote mRNA decay. Small interfering RNAs act similarly in RNA interference.

Long non-coding RNAs are longer than 200 nucleotides; they can guide chromatin-modifying proteins to particular genes. Riboswitches are RNA elements that change shape when they bind a small molecule and then control transcription or translation, mainly in bacteria. These mechanisms let cells respond quickly without making new proteins.

keyPoints: Operons group genes under one promoter and control them with repressors and activators.
Transcription factors bind DNA and regulate transcription, often combinatorially.
Chromatin remodelling and histone modification change how accessible DNA is.
DNA methylation and some histone marks are epigenetic and can be copied through cell division.
MicroRNAs and siRNAs reduce mRNA translation or stability, while long non-coding RNAs can guide chromatin changes.
The lac operon, X-chromosome inactivation and hormone receptors are standard examples of regulated expression.

en.title: Membrane transport and signal transduction
en.short: Passive and active transport, pumps, channels, receptors, second messengers and main signalling pathways.

sections.heading: Passive transport
sections.text: Passive transport moves solutes down their electrochemical gradient without metabolic energy. Simple diffusion crosses the lipid bilayer; facilitated diffusion uses channels or carriers. Ion channels are selective and often gated. The membrane potential arises from unequal ion distributions and selective permeability. The Nernst equation gives an ion’s equilibrium potential: E = (61.5 mV) log10([ion]out ÷ [ion]in) at 37 °C for a monovalent cation. For K+ with 5 mM outside and 140 mM inside, E = 61.5 × log10(5 ÷ 140) = −89 mV. This is close to the resting potential of many cells.

sections.heading: Active transport
sections.text: Active transport moves solutes against their gradient and needs energy. Primary active transport uses ATP directly. The Na+/K+ ATPase pumps three Na+ out and two K+ in per ATP hydrolysed, keeping Na+ low and K+ high. It is electrogenic and helps set the resting potential. Secondary active transport uses the Na+ gradient. Symporters move Na+ and another solute the same way, as in SGLT glucose uptake; antiporters move them in opposite directions, as in Na+/Ca2+ exchange. ABC transporters use ATP to move diverse substrates.

sections.heading: Receptors and messengers
sections.text: Receptors detect signals and convert them into cellular responses. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) span the membrane seven times and activate heterotrimeric G proteins. Ligand binding exchanges GDP for GTP on the Gα subunit, which then regulates effectors such as adenylyl cyclase. Second messengers are small intracellular molecules that amplify the signal. cAMP is made from ATP by adenylyl cyclase and activates protein kinase A (PKA). Other second messengers include Ca2+, inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG).

sections.heading: Main pathways
sections.text: Receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) dimerise on ligand binding and autophosphorylate. They recruit proteins with SH2 domains, including Grb2, which recruits SOS to activate Ras. Ras then activates the MAP kinase cascade (Raf, MEK, ERK), controlling growth. The insulin receptor is an RTK and signals through insulin receptor substrate (IRS) proteins. GPCR pathways include the cAMP/PKA route and the phospholipase C/IP3/DAG route, which releases Ca2+ and activates protein kinase C. Signalling is switched off by phosphatases, phosphodiesterases and GTPase activity.

keyPoints: Passive transport uses diffusion, channels or carriers and needs no ATP.
The Nernst equation E = 61.5 log10([ion]out ÷ [ion]in) mV at 37 °C gives a monovalent cation’s equilibrium potential.
The Na+/K+ ATPase uses one ATP to pump 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, keeping Na+ low and K+ high.
GPCRs activate G proteins, which switch on effectors such as adenylyl cyclase and phospholipase C.
cAMP, Ca2+, IP3 and DAG are second messengers that amplify and spread a signal.
RTKs autophosphorylate and signal through Ras and the MAP kinase cascade; phosphatases and phosphodiesterases switch signals off.

en.title: Biochemical techniques: extraction, separation and detection
en.short: Extraction, centrifugation, chromatography, electrophoresis, spectroscopy, immunoassays and mass spectrometry.

sections.heading: Extraction and centrifugation
sections.text:
Proteins are extracted in a buffer of controlled pH and ionic strength, often with protease inhibitors and a detergent to break membranes. Metabolites are extracted by quenching (rapidly stopping) metabolism, then using a solvent such as cold methanol or perchloric acid; the choice depends on whether the metabolite is polar or lipid-soluble.

After extraction, centrifugation separates particles by size and density. The relative centrifugal force (RCF) is RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × (rpm)², with r in centimetres. For example, r = 10 cm and 12,000 rpm gives RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × 10 × 1.44 × 10⁸ = about 16,100 × g.

sections.heading: Chromatography and electrophoresis
sections.text:
Chromatography separates molecules between a mobile phase and a stationary phase. In size-exclusion chromatography, large proteins enter the pores less and elute first; in ion-exchange, binding depends on charge; in affinity chromatography, a specific ligand captures the target.

Electrophoresis separates charged molecules in an electric field. SDS-PAGE denatures proteins and separates them mainly by mass, while native PAGE keeps shape and charge. Isoelectric focusing separates by isoelectric point.

sections.heading: Spectroscopy and immunoassays
sections.text:
Spectroscopy measures how molecules absorb or emit light. The Beer-Lambert law is A = εcl, where A is absorbance, ε is the molar absorption coefficient, c is concentration and l is path length.

Example: if A = 0.45, ε = 15,000 M⁻¹ cm⁻¹ and l = 1 cm, then c = 0.45 ÷ (15,000 × 1) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ M.

Immunoassays use antibodies to detect specific proteins or small molecules. ELISA is common: an enzyme label produces a colour whose intensity is proportional to the analyte.

sections.heading: Mass spectrometry
sections.text: Mass spectrometry ionises molecules, separates the ions by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) and detects them. It gives molecular mass and, with fragmentation, structural information. It is very sensitive and is used for proteomics and metabolite profiling. Coupling it to chromatography (LC-MS or GC-MS) adds separation before detection.

keyPoints: Centrifugation force: RCF = 1.118 × 10⁻⁵ × r × (rpm)², with r in cm.
Beer-Lambert law: A = εcl; absorbance is proportional to concentration at fixed path length.
Chromatography separates by differential partitioning between mobile and stationary phases.
SDS-PAGE separates denatured proteins mainly by mass.
Immunoassays use antibody binding, often with an enzyme label such as ELISA.
Mass spectrometry measures m/z and is often coupled to chromatography.

en.title: Molecular biology techniques
en.short: Restriction enzymes, cloning, PCR, sequencing, blotting, CRISPR and recombinant protein expression.

sections.heading: Cutting and cloning
sections.text: Restriction enzymes are bacterial enzymes that cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, often palindromic. Many leave sticky ends, short single-stranded overhangs that base-pair with a compatible insert; DNA ligase then joins the backbones. In cloning, a DNA fragment is inserted into a vector, a carrier DNA molecule such as a plasmid, and put into host cells by transformation. Selection markers, often antibiotic-resistance genes, identify cells that took up the vector. Limitations: useful sites may be absent or repeated, and cutting can occur elsewhere.

sections.heading: PCR and sequencing
sections.text: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) copies a chosen DNA region using two primers, short DNA sequences flanking the target, a thermostable DNA polymerase, nucleotides and repeated heating and cooling. Denaturation separates strands, annealing lets primers bind, extension copies the template. Yield grows about 2^n until reagents run out. Example: one target molecule after 20 cycles gives 2^20 = 1,048,576 copies, but real reactions plateau and errors occur. PCR is used in diagnosis, cloning and forensics. DNA sequencing finds base order. Sanger sequencing uses chain-terminating dideoxynucleotides and capillary electrophoresis; next-generation methods read many fragments in parallel. Limitations: short reads, errors, and need for a reference or assembly.

sections.heading: Blotting and CRISPR
sections.text: Blotting transfers separated DNA, RNA or protein to a membrane and detects one molecule with a labelled probe or antibody: Southern for DNA, Northern for RNA, Western for protein. It shows presence and size but is semi-quantitative. CRISPR-Cas9 is gene editing: a guide RNA directs the Cas9 nuclease to a complementary DNA sequence, making a double-strand break. Repair can disable a gene or, with a template, insert a change. Uses include research models and crop improvement. Limits include off-target cuts, delivery problems and ethical rules that vary by country.

sections.heading: Protein expression
sections.text: Recombinant protein expression places a coding sequence in an expression vector with a promoter, then introduces it into host cells such as Escherichia coli, yeast or mammalian cells. Tags help purification. Uses include therapeutic insulin and enzymes.
