Limits: bacteria cannot perform many human post-translational modifications, proteins may misfold or form inclusion bodies, and yields vary.

keyPoints: Restriction enzymes cut specific DNA sequences; DNA ligase joins fragments during cloning.
PCR yield is about initial copies × 2^n, but plateau and errors limit it.
Sanger sequencing uses chain-terminating dideoxynucleotides; next-generation sequencing reads many fragments in parallel.
Southern, Northern and Western blotting detect DNA, RNA and protein respectively.
CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to target Cas9 cutting; off-target effects and delivery are main limits.
Recombinant proteins need suitable hosts because post-translational modifications and folding differ.

en.title: Metabolic integration and clinical biochemistry
en.short: Hormonal control of fed, fasted and exercise metabolism, diabetes, metabolic disorders and diagnostic tests.

sections.heading: Fed and fasted
sections.text:
Metabolic integration means the body matching fuel supply to demand across tissues. In the fed state, high insulin and low glucagon favour storage: insulin promotes glucose uptake in muscle and adipose tissue, glycogen synthesis, lipogenesis and protein synthesis, and suppresses gluconeogenesis and ketogenesis. The liver stores glucose as glycogen and converts excess to fat.

In fasting, insulin falls and glucagon rises, with cortisol, adrenaline and growth hormone helping. Glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis maintain blood glucose for the brain and red cells. Lipolysis releases fatty acids; the liver makes ketones for the brain and muscle. Prolonged fasting increases ketone use and reduces glucose demand.

sections.heading: Exercise
sections.text: Exercise is a controlled fast in the working muscle. Adrenaline and glucagon rise and insulin falls. Muscle uses its own glycogen and blood glucose; liver glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis supply glucose. After exercise, insulin returns to refill glycogen. Training increases mitochondrial enzymes and fat use, sparing glycogen.

sections.heading: Metabolic disorders
sections.text:
Diabetes mellitus is chronic hyperglycaemia from insulin deficiency or resistance. Type 1 is absolute insulin deficiency and can cause diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), with hyperglycaemia, ketones and acidosis. Type 2 is insulin resistance with relative deficiency and risks hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state. Other disorders include hypoglycaemia, dyslipidaemias, gout, phenylketonuria and glycogen storage diseases.

Case: Chidi, a student, presents with thirst, weight loss and deep breathing. Urine ketones are positive and blood gas shows acidosis. This pattern suggests DKA; treatment needs fluids, insulin and electrolyte monitoring in hospital.

sections.heading: Diagnostic tests
sections.text:
Biochemical tests support diagnosis and monitoring. Plasma glucose, oral glucose tolerance tests and HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) assess glycaemia; HbA1c reflects average glucose over the red cell lifespan. Ketones, electrolytes, blood gases and renal function assess acute diabetes. Lipid profile, uric acid, liver and kidney tests and urine albumin screen for complications. Enzyme assays and newborn screening detect inherited disorders.

Interpret tests with preanalytical care: fasting status, haemolysis and delay affect results. Reference intervals and diagnostic cutoffs vary by laboratory, guideline and country; always check the local source.

keyPoints: In the fed state, high insulin favours storage and low glucagon reduces glucose output.
In fasting, low insulin and high glucagon drive glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and ketogenesis.
Exercise raises adrenaline and glucagon and lowers insulin, mobilising muscle and liver glycogen.
Type 1 diabetes is absolute insulin deficiency with DKA risk; type 2 is insulin resistance with relative deficiency.
HbA1c reflects average glycaemia, while ketones, electrolytes and blood gases assess acute metabolic decompensation.
Diagnostic cutoffs and reference intervals vary by guideline and country, so check the current local source.

en.title: Research ethics and biosafety in biochemistry
en.short: Ethical conduct, consent, animal use, data integrity, biosafety levels, risk assessment and waste disposal.

sections.heading: Consent and approval
sections.text:
Biochemical research with people or their samples needs approval from an ethics committee before work starts. Informed consent means the person understands the purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives, takes part freely and may withdraw. Consent should be documented, and samples and data kept confidential.

Leftover clinical samples are not free for any new test: using them usually needs consent or an approved waiver. Rules differ by country and institution, so check local requirements.

sections.heading: Animal use
sections.text:
Animal experiments require approval by an animal ethics committee and trained staff. The 3Rs guide humane design: replacement (use cells or models where possible), reduction (use the fewest animals that give valid results) and refinement (reduce pain and distress).

Use anaesthesia and analgesia when needed, set humane endpoints, and keep records. The legal rules vary by country.

sections.heading: Data integrity
sections.text:
Data integrity means records are complete, accurate and traceable. Fabrication is inventing data; falsification is changing or omitting results; plagiarism is using others’ words or ideas without credit. Keep raw data and a dated lab notebook, and store electronic files securely.

Case: Amina sees a classmate reuse the same blot image in two figures. She should report it to the supervisor or integrity office, not edit it herself. Authorship needs real contribution.

sections.heading: Biosafety and waste
sections.text:
Biosafety levels (BSL-1 to BSL-4) set containment that rises with hazard. BSL-1 suits low-risk agents; BSL-2 adds controls for moderate risk; BSL-3 and BSL-4 are for serious hazards. Risk assessment identifies the agent, exposure route, likelihood and severity, then applies controls: engineering, practice, protective equipment.

Waste is segregated at source. Biological waste is autoclaved or incinerated, sharps go in rigid containers, and chemical waste is kept separate. Follow national and institutional rules.

keyPoints: Get ethics committee approval and informed consent before human research.
Animal work needs animal ethics approval and follows the 3Rs.
Data integrity forbids fabrication, falsification and plagiarism.
Biosafety levels rise from BSL-1 to BSL-4 with the hazard.
Risk assessment identifies hazards and exposure routes before controls are chosen.
Segregate waste at source and follow national and institutional rules.

en.title: Advanced enzymology and protein dynamics
en.short: Pre-steady-state kinetics, catalytic mechanisms, allostery, folding, dynamics and biophysical methods.

sections.heading: Kinetics beyond steady state
sections.text:
Steady-state kinetics measures initial rates after the enzyme-substrate complex reaches a constant level. It gives kcat, Km and the specificity constant kcat/Km. Pre-steady-state kinetics resolves the steps before that plateau, often with stopped-flow or rapid quench.

For simple binding, kobs = k1[S] + k−1. A plot of kobs against [S] has slope k1 and intercept k−1. Example: at [S] = 20 µM, kobs = 220 s−1; at [S] = 50 µM, kobs = 400 s−1. Slope = (400 − 220) ÷ (50 − 20) = 6 s−1 µM−1 = 6 × 10⁶ M−1 s−1. Intercept = 220 − 6 × 20 = 100 s−1.

sections.heading: Catalysis and allostery
sections.text:
Catalysis lowers activation energy by stabilising the transition state. Common devices are acid-base catalysis, covalent catalysis, metal-ion catalysis, and proximity or orientation effects. Each is defined by the species or interaction that speeds the reaction.

Allostery is control from a site remote from the active site. The MWC model treats the protein as switching concertedly between T and R states; the KNF model allows sequential changes. The Hill coefficient nH is greater than 1 for positive cooperativity, less than 1 for negative cooperativity, and near 1 without cooperativity. Homotropic effects come from the substrate; heterotropic effects come from other modulators.

sections.heading: Folding, dynamics and methods
sections.text:
Folding is described by an energy landscape, not one fixed path. Anfinsen showed that sequence can determine the native state; the Levinthal paradox is resolved because the landscape funnels the chain towards native contacts. Chaperones assist folding in the cell, and molten globules are partly folded intermediates.

Dynamics means proteins exist as conformational ensembles, with side-chain, loop and domain motions from nanoseconds to milliseconds. Intrinsically disordered proteins lack a fixed structure but can fold on binding. Methods are chosen by timescale and property: stopped-flow and rapid quench for pre-steady-state steps, surface plasmon resonance for binding kinetics, isothermal titration calorimetry for binding enthalpy, circular dichroism and fluorescence for folding, NMR for dynamics, and cryo-electron microscopy or small-angle X-ray scattering for structure.

keyPoints: Steady-state kinetics gives kcat and Km; kcat/Km measures catalytic efficiency.
Pre-steady-state kobs = k1[S] + k−1 for simple binding; slope gives k1 and intercept k−1.
Catalysis uses transition-state stabilisation plus acid-base, covalent, metal-ion and proximity effects.
MWC is concerted and KNF is sequential; nH greater than 1 indicates positive cooperativity.
Folding follows an energy landscape, and chaperones assist folding in the cell.
Stopped-flow, NMR, ITC, CD and cryo-EM probe different timescales and properties.

en.title: Genomics, proteomics and bioinformatics
en.short: High-throughput sequencing, omics data, database search, alignment and large-data statistics.

sections.heading: Sequencing and assembly
sections.text:
High-throughput sequencing reads DNA or RNA in parallel, producing millions of short reads. Coverage is the average number of times each base is read: coverage = total bases sequenced ÷ genome size.

Example: 1,000,000 reads of 150 bp give 150,000,000 bases; over a 5,000,000 bp genome, coverage = 150,000,000 ÷ 5,000,000 = 30×. Reads are aligned to a reference or assembled de novo (without a reference), then variants are called and expression levels are estimated. Long reads help with repeats but err more.

sections.heading: Proteomics and metabolomics
sections.text:
Proteomics identifies and quantifies proteins, usually by digesting them into peptides, separating them by liquid chromatography and measuring them by tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Metabolomics measures small molecules in a sample, often by mass spectrometry or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Both produce large peak lists.

Identification depends on database searching: software compares each experimental spectrum with theoretical or reference spectra from databases (protein sequences for peptides, spectral libraries for metabolites) and scores the match. Quantification, normalisation and quality control are needed before interpretation.

sections.heading: Alignment and database search
sections.text:
Sequence alignment places two or more sequences side by side to find homology. Pairwise alignment can be global (whole length) or local (best region). It uses a substitution matrix and gap penalties.

BLAST is a heuristic local search that finds similar sequences quickly in a database. The E-value is the expected number of hits with that score or better by chance; a lower E-value is stronger evidence. Multiple alignment and profile hidden Markov models extend this to families. Example: two 20-base reads with 18 matches and 2 mismatches have identity 18 ÷ 20 × 100 = 90%.

sections.heading: Statistics and computation
sections.text:
Large biological datasets need statistics. Multiple testing is a problem: testing thousands of genes or peptides produces false positives unless the false discovery rate (FDR) is controlled, for example by the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Normalisation removes technical variation; batch effects must be modelled.

Reproducible pipelines record software versions and parameters. Machine learning can classify samples, but validation on independent data is essential. Results should be shared with raw data and code.

keyPoints: Coverage = total bases sequenced ÷ genome size; 1,000,000 reads × 150 bp over 5 Mb gives 30×.
High-throughput sequencing produces short reads that are aligned to a reference or assembled de novo before variant calling.
Proteomics mainly uses LC-MS/MS with protein sequence databases; metabolomics often uses mass spectrometry or NMR with spectral libraries.
BLAST is a heuristic local alignment search; the E-value is the expected number of chance hits, so lower is better.
Multiple testing must be controlled, often by false discovery rate, to avoid false positives in omics data.
Reproducible analysis records software versions, parameters, raw data and code.

en.title: Research methods in biochemistry
en.short: Literature review, experimental design, sampling, statistics, reproducibility, ethics approval and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Literature review
sections.text: A literature review is a structured search and critical appraisal of existing evidence, not a list of papers. Define the question, choose databases such as PubMed or Web of Science, record search terms and inclusion criteria, and read primary papers alongside reviews. Use a reference manager and cite every source. A good review states what is known, what is contested and what gap your study addresses. Check access through your institution; database coverage varies.

sections.heading: Design and sampling
sections.text: Experimental design turns a hypothesis into a testable plan. State the question, primary outcome, controls, replication and the comparison groups before collecting data. Randomise where possible, blind where bias is likely, and identify confounders. Sampling must be representative of the population you claim to study; convenience samples limit generalisation. Sample size depends on effect size, variability, power and significance level, so use a power calculation or a statistician’s advice rather than a rule of thumb.

sections.heading: Statistics and reproducibility
sections.text: Pre-specify the statistical analysis. Report means with standard deviation (SD) for spread or standard error (SEM) for precision of a mean, and give confidence intervals. A p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme if the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true. Example: replicate activities 2.0, 2.2 and 2.4 U/mL give mean 2.2 U/mL and SD = √(0.08 ÷ 2) = 0.20 U/mL; n = 3 is too small for a claim. Reproducibility needs standard operating procedures, biological and technical replicates, raw data, metadata and reporting guidelines.

sections.heading: Ethics and dissertation
sections.text: Research ethics approval is required before human, animal or hazardous work. Submit the protocol to your institutional review board or ethics committee; for human studies, obtain informed consent and protect personal data. Rules differ by country and institution, so check the current local requirements. The dissertation is usually written in IMRaD form: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion. Present figures with labelled axes, state limitations, follow the required referencing style and keep a data trail for examination.

keyPoints: A literature review is a reproducible search with explicit inclusion criteria and critical appraisal, not a list of papers.
Define the primary outcome, controls, randomisation and sample size before data collection.
Sample size should follow an effect size and power calculation, not a fixed rule.
Mean = Σx ÷ n and sample SD = √(Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1)).
A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true; report confidence intervals and pre-specified analyses.
Ethics approval and informed consent are required before the work starts; standard operating procedures and a complete data trail are required before submission and examination.
